core: working definition of an economic system: an economy is a system for making, circulating, and using things (goods, services, information) and the central way societies meet basic material needs and wants; economic systems are shaped by ideas about the meaning and value of objects, actions, and people (attributed to OpenStax Introduction to Anthropology ch. 7)
production: four classic modes with one line each — foragers (gatherer-hunters), horticulturalists, pastoralists, agriculturalists; depth deferred to the sibling subsistence topic
distribution: three forms — reciprocity, redistribution, market exchange — each with one line and an original example, framed by Polanyi's three-forms map and Mauss's gift work
the gift idea: gift exchange builds and expresses relationships, not just value; the obligations to give, receive, and return (attributed to Marcel Mauss, The Gift)
consumption: what people do with goods — using them — one line, stated simply
the embedded-economy idea: the economy is embedded in society (kinship, religion, politics), not a separate sphere (attributed to Karl Polanyi)
the honest framing: economies are social arrangements, not just markets; anthropologists describe what people think and do as they make a living without ranking practices
supporting: money as the usual medium of market exchange (three functions noted in passing)
the contrast between economic anthropology and the discipline of economics (universalist models vs. human-centered cultural description)
outOfScope: detailed treatment of modes of subsistence (sibling topic anthropology:foundations:subsistence)
market theory, supply and demand, price formation (owned by the economics subject)
barter debates and the history of money (economics subject)

claims.claim: An economy is a system for making, circulating, and using things — material goods, services, and information — and is the central way a society meets its basic material needs and wants; economic systems are shaped by ideas about the meaning and value of objects, actions, and people.

Production is organized around four classic modes: gathering-hunting (foraging), pastoralism, plant cultivation, and industrialism; horticulture and agriculture are distinct strategies of plant cultivation; each mode also organizes society to get the necessary work done.

Reciprocity is a form of distribution in which goods and services move between people with an expected but usually uncalculated return: generalized reciprocity is sharing without tracking value (egalitarian sharing in gatherer-hunter bands, families, friendships), and balanced reciprocity involves return gifts of roughly equal or slightly greater value whose worth and timing are never discussed (e.g., hxaro gift relationships).

Redistribution is a form of distribution in which goods flow toward a center — a chief, leader, or state — and are given out again: chiefs who control community wealth (precolonial Hawaiian Islands), potlatch feasts, and taxation that funds roads, schools, and libraries in state societies.

Market exchange is a form of distribution in which buyers and sellers of goods transact through a market institution, typically using money; market transactions are quick and participants walk away relatively unencumbered by future obligation.

The gift idea (Mauss): Marcel Mauss made the first extended application of gift exchange to social life, stressing its social side rather than its economic functions; the gift cycle entails obligations to give, to receive, and to return; refusing to give or take can read as refusing alliance; the profit of gift exchange lies in social relationships and prestige rather than material advantage.

The embedded-economy idea (Polanyi): Karl Polanyi argued that economies are embedded in society — in non-market societies economic activities such as provisioning run through kinship, religious, and political institutions, and true market exchange was limited to a restricted number of western industrial societies; in market societies economic activity became more separate (disembedded).

Consumption is the part of an economy in which people use goods, and because economic systems are shaped by ideas about the meaning and value of things, using is also cultural — the same good can carry different meanings in different households.

Honest framing: anthropologists take a human-centered approach to economic issues, describing what people think and do as they make a living and how practices are shaped by culture and history, without ranking economic practices as better or worse against an ideal; reciprocity, redistribution, and market exchange coexist in contemporary societies.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many main forms of distribution are there, and who is credited with the map?
positions: Polanyi's framework (as summarized by Wikipedia's economic-anthropology article) treats reciprocity, redistribution, and market exchange as the main forms, and argues true market exchange was historically limited to a restricted number of western industrial societies.

OpenStax 7.6 describes generalized and balanced reciprocity, redistribution, and market exchange in detail, and also discusses money, barter, and the claim that precapitalist peoples relied more on gift exchange, redistribution, and debt than on barter.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names the three classic forms — reciprocity, redistribution, and market exchange — attributed to Polanyi's framework with Mauss's gift work underlying reciprocity, using OpenStax's descriptions as the factual backbone. Money, barter, and market theory are left to the economics subject.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does the economic-systems topic include production, or is production owned by the subsistence topic?
positions: OpenStax defines the economy as making, circulating, and using things, so production is part of the economy.
The curriculum assigns detailed modes-of-subsistence study to the sibling topic anthropology:foundations:subsistence.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson covers production in one line per mode (foragers, horticulturalists, pastoralists, agriculturalists) and defers depth — how each mode works, its history, its cultural forms — to the sibling subsistence topic.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A anchor. New id minted (no phase-2/3/4 registry entry for chapter 7). OpenStax blocks direct fetch; read 2026-08-22 via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical URL (web.archive.org/web/20250201044859/https://openstax.org/books/introduction-anthropology/pages/7-introduction). Supports: the working definition — an economy is the central way in which societies meet basic material needs and wants; more specifically, a system for making, circulating, and using things (material goods, services, information); economic systems are shaped by ideas about the meaning and value of objects, actions, and people; anthropologists of all four fields study how people make a living.

sourceRecords.title: 7.2 Modes of Subsistence — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. New id minted. Read 2026-08-22 via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical URL (web.archive.org/web/20241202015414/https://openstax.org/books/introduction-anthropology/pages/7-2-modes-of-subsistence). Supports the one-line production classification: four main modes of subsistence — gathering-hunting, pastoralism, plant cultivation, and industrialism/post-industrialism; each mode incorporates distinctive strategies for producing, exchanging, and consuming; modes also organize society to get the necessary work done. Detailed subsistence study is the sibling topic's job; this lesson uses only the one-line classification.

sourceRecords.title: 7.6 Exchange, Value, and Consumption — Introduction to Anthropology (OpenStax)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. New id minted. Read 2026-08-22 via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical URL (web.archive.org/web/20241126232703/https://openstax.org/books/introduction-anthropology/pages/7-6-exchange-value-and-consumption). Supports: generalized reciprocity (egalitarian sharing in gatherer-hunter bands and among family/friends), balanced reciprocity (hxaro gift relationships; return gift of equal or slightly greater value, value and timing never discussed), potlatch feasts, redistribution (leaders controlling community wealth; precolonial Hawaiian Islands; taxation funding roads, schools, libraries), market exchange (an institution enabling buyers and sellers; West African markets; transactions quick and participants unencumbered by future obligation), money's three functions, and the claim that precapitalist peoples relied more on gift exchange, redistribution, and debt than on barter.

sourceRecords.title: Do the Olympics Make Economic Sense?
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (SAPIENS, anthropology explainer magazine of the Wenner-Gren Foundation). New id minted; read live 2026-08-22 via direct HTTP fetch. Essay applying the gift-economy concept to the Olympic Games. Supports the gift idea: the 'gift economy' in which material goods, labor, services, hospitality, dances, and even rituals and festivals are exchanged; creditworthiness measured by a person's reputation and honor; bonds of trust between givers and receivers that strengthen solidarity; Marcel Mauss, who introduced the concept in The Gift, observing that to refuse to give, to neglect to invite, as to refuse to take, is equivalent to declaring war — it is to refuse alliance and communion; Mauss's emphasis on hospitality.

sourceRecords.title: Gift Exchange
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. New id minted. Britannica blocks automated fetch; read 2026-08-22 via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical URL (web.archive.org/web/20230207044328/https://www.britannica.com/topic/gift-exchange). Supports: gift exchange (also called ceremonial exchange) as the transfer of goods or services regarded as voluntary but carrying an expected return; the gift-exchange cycle entailing obligations to give, to receive, and to return; refusal to accept a gift seen as refusal of social relations; Marcel Mauss making the first extended application of gift exchange to social life, stressing social concomitants rather than economic functions; the profit of gift exchange lying in social relationships and prestige rather than material advantage; gift exchange expressing or establishing a social relationship unlike impersonal market relationships.

sourceRecords.title: Economic Anthropology
sourceRecords.notes: Tier D tertiary. New id minted; read live 2026-08-22 via the MediaWiki API (plain-text extract). Used only for the Polanyi attributions: economic historian Karl Polanyi drew on anthropological studies to argue that true market exchange was limited to a restricted number of western, industrial societies; in non-industrial societies exchange was 'embedded' in such non-market institutions as kinship, religion, and politics (an idea he borrowed from Mauss); he labelled this approach substantivism; Mauss's The Gift (Essai sur le don, 1925) is the origin of anthropological studies of reciprocity, and Malinowski and Mauss founded the subfield on the nature of reciprocity as an alternative to market exchange.

sourceRecords.title: Substantivism
sourceRecords.notes: Tier D tertiary. New id minted; read live 2026-08-22 via the MediaWiki API (plain-text extract). Supports the embedded-economy claim: substantivism first proposed by Karl Polanyi; Polanyi argued that in non-market societies there are no pure economic institutions to which formal economic models can be applied, and economic activities such as provisioning are embedded in non-economic kinship, religious, and political institutions; in market societies economic activities have become more separate (disembedded).
